meta.title: The NAAC Value Chain
meta.description: From radio audio to safe cockpit action — where value is created, gated, and currently lost

props.title: The Value Chain
props.subtitle: From a crackly radio transmission to a safe, FAA-legal cockpit action

props.content: One product moment defines everything we build: ATC says something on frequency, and our system must (a) understand it, (b) decide whether it carries authority for our aircraft, (c) hand the flight management module a correct typed command, and (d) speak back a correct readback. Every corpus, gate, and parser exists to make that moment provably reliable. This page walks the chain end to end and shows exactly where value is created, how it is measured, and where it is leaking today.

The value is delivered at the two gold endpoints: the audio coming in and the readback going out. Everything between them is either **understanding** (ASR, parsing), **authority** (addressing filter, FMM decision), or **speech** (readback policy, TTS).

Two design laws shape the whole chain. First, **nothing speaks without FMM authority** — a parse alone never produces a transmission; it produces a typed proposal that the flight management module approves or rejects. Second, **the chain fails closed** — if any stage can't produce an honest result, the system asks the controller to say again rather than guessing. A wrong readback in the air is far worse than a repeated question.

props.label: STAGE BY STAGE
props.title: Where value is created — and lost
props.subtitle: Each link adds value; each link can destroy it

props.title: 🎙️ 1 · Speech to text
props.content: An ATC-finetuned Whisper model turns radio audio into a transcript. Value created: everything downstream is possible. Value lost: THIS is where today's biggest leak enters — phonetic garble. The same audio that reads perfectly on paper comes out as 'CLEARED TOUCH AND GEO' or 'LOWE S ANGELS'. Every downstream stage inherits that damage.

props.title: 📡 2 · Addressing filter
props.content: Radio is a party line. The filter decides: addressed to us, addressed to someone else, or a broadcast. Value created: we never act on another aircraft's clearance and never go deaf to all-aircraft safety calls. Value lost if wrong: acting on someone else's instruction — the worst possible failure — so this gate is deliberately conservative.

props.title: 🧩 3 · Intent parse
props.content: The transcript becomes a typed intent plus slots ('descend and maintain 3,000' → altitude_change, altitude=3000). Two parsers run side by side: the regex parser carries production; the template grammar — compiled from ~500 FAA phraseology rows — runs in shadow on every same turn, so we can compare them row by row without risking the live lane.

props.title: 🛡️ 4 · FMM authority
props.content: The parse becomes a typed command proposal with executable parameters. The flight management module (a stand-in until Phase 3) approves or rejects it. Value created: a machine-actionable command the aircraft can trust. Anti-cheat law: every ownship command that survives the earlier gates MUST reach FMM as a proposal — silence here is a bug, not a pass.

props.title: 🗣️ 5 · Readback + speech
props.content: Policy selects the FAA-legal readback for the approved command, and TTS transmits it in the pilot's voice. Value delivered: the controller hears exactly what a competent human pilot would say, closing the loop. An empty or wrong readback is suppressed and escalated — never improvised.

props.title: 🔁 6 · The say-again lane
props.content: When parsing fails honestly, the system asks the controller to repeat — exactly what a human pilot does. This is a real value path, not a failure bucket: a say-again costs a few seconds; a guessed readback can cost an incident. The open work is making sure garbled turns actually route here instead of being silently dropped.

props.content: The pairing that matters most is **B1 vs B2**: the same 500-odd rows, once through real audio and ASR, once with perfect text. A row that passes B2 but fails B1 is a **twin gap** — proof the grammar is right and the ASR text is what broke it. That single comparison is what separates 'the parser is missing coverage' from 'the transcript is garbled', and it is why we never chase a failure without checking its twin first.

props.label: GATING
props.title: Why progress looks slow and is real
props.subtitle: Kill-test first: the bar is set before the experiment runs

props.content:
Every proposed improvement runs as a **kill-test**: pass/fail thresholds are pinned in writing BEFORE anything is measured, the change runs in an isolated worktree, and a full-corpus comparison decides GO or NO_GO. A NO_GO is a successful outcome — it closes a dead end permanently with a receipt, so no future session re-explores it.

The fences exist because the regex lane once got its numbers by quietly fitting the answer key — rows written to match specific eval transcripts. Those wins evaporate on any new audio. So today: no corpus-verbatim rows, no ML deciding acceptance, no scoring-tool edits riding along with a change, and a zero-lexical-evidence law — a parse that only survived by repair-deleting all its literal words may not claim an intent.

Four experiments in the grammar family have now been honestly killed: candidate re-ranking, facility-prefix stripping, island anchor-floor tuning, and authoring 44 more FAA-grounded rows (recovered only 5 — honest FAA phrasing cannot match garbled fragments). Each NO_GO narrowed the search: the remaining loss is not a coverage problem, it is an ASR-robustness problem.

props.title: The anti-cheat principle
props.content: A competent optimizer will always find the cheapest path to a green number — memorizing the eval, editing the scorer, shrinking the denominator. Every gate here (pinned thresholds, frozen held-out sets, full-denominator wrong-accept counts, receipts with hashes) exists to make genuine capability cheaper than cheating.

props.label: THE PARSER BET
props.title: Regex today, grammar tomorrow
props.subtitle: Why two parsers run on every turn

props.title: Regex parser — production
props.content: Carries the live lane today. Battle-tested, but its patterns were historically written against the eval corpus, so its coverage is partly memorized rather than generalized. Adding a new phrase means hand-writing a new pattern. It is the floor we must never regress.

props.title: Template grammar — shadow
props.content: An Earley chart parser compiled from ~500 FAA-grounded phraseology rows. Generative by construction: new coverage comes from adding a grounded data row, not code. Perfect on clean text (476/476) and on the frozen held-out set (31/31). It runs in shadow on every turn; promotion to production happens only when head-to-head comparison proves no scored row moves backward. Its one open weakness — and the current frontier — is garbled ASR text.

props.label: THE LEAK
props.title: Where value is escaping right now
props.subtitle: The twin gap is the whole story

props.content:
Take one real fixture: the audio for a straight-in approach clearance. On perfect text the grammar parses it to gold. The ATC-finetuned Whisper hears **'STRAIGHT AND'** for *straight-in*, **'CLEARED TOUCH AND GEO'** for *touch and go*, **'3 000'** split across tokens. The grammar — correctly refusing to hallucinate — fails the turn, and the turn either forfeits to a wrong intent or drops.

Every cheap fix has been kill-tested and buried. What remains are the structural options: matching words by sound instead of spelling, pricing repairs from our own measured ASR confusion pairs, or parsing the recognizer's alternatives (lattice) instead of its single best guess. That decision is exactly what the exported consultation bundle asks — with the entire engine, all 500 template rows, and 535 measured perfect-vs-whisper pairs attached as evidence.

props.title: Value chain, one sentence
props.content: Audio becomes text (Thor Whisper) → text becomes a typed intent (regex live, grammar shadow) → intent becomes an authorized command (FMM gate) → command becomes a spoken readback (policy + TTS) — and 'just baseline' scores every link on 2,020 rows so no link can lie about its contribution.

props.title: 1 · ASR-robustness decision
props.content: Pick the mechanism that closes the twin gap — phonetic terminal matching, confusion-mined repair pricing, or lattice-input parsing. The full-context bundle (engine + rows + evidence + kill-test findings) is exported and ready to hand to an outside oracle. Whatever comes back gets the same kill-test treatment as everything else.

props.title: 2 · Two missing value domains
props.content: Recent gold corrections introduced two command parameters ('fix or distance' and 'parking') that have no declared legal value ranges yet. It is the last red light on the infrastructure panel — a small, fully-scoped data fix that restores an all-green gate.

props.title: 3 · Move the pilot phrasebook out
props.content: The demo console's fake-Siri pilot phrases still physically live inside the FAA phraseology surface, held out of the pipeline by two hand-maintained skip lists. Migrating them to a gateway-owned home deletes both hacks and closes a standing 'this will fuck us later' risk.
